text: This is NEWS & NOTES.  I'm Farai Chideya.

Over the weekend, Chief Justice William Hubbs Rehnquist died at his home      in Virginia.  He was 80.  And today, President Bush nominated Judge John      Roberts to replace him.  Roberts was previously nominated to replace      retiring Justice Sandra Day O'Connor.  Joining us to talk about the      court's 16th chief justice and African-Americans are Harvard law      Professor Charles Ogletree and Ted Shaw, president and director-counsel      for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.
Gentlemen, thank you so much and welcome.
Hello, Farai.  Good to      be with you.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Thank you.  Good to be with you.

So we want to spend some time on the legacy of Justice      Rehnquist, but first, let's ask the big question:  Why has Judge Roberts,      who until today was just a nominee for an associate justice, been so      swiftly moved to the front of the line for chief justice?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, I think it makes sense from the administration's point      of view.  They wanted to have somebody in place by the first Monday in      October, when the court begins its new term.  And they don't want the      court coming into session without new leadership that they have chosen.      If they did not replace Chief Justice Rehnquist, then Justice Stevens      would be the acting chief justice.  I don't think that's something they      want, and they don't want the vacancy, period.  In terms of Justice      Roberts' re-nomination for chief justice, it's not really a surprise.  I      think that there were three options. One was to elevate one of the      current sitting associate justices.  The other was to nominate somebody      fresh to be chief.  But John Roberts is a known quantity, he's been      vetted, and they have a lot of confidence in his intellectual ability,      and he's going to be on the court for 30 years, if he's confirmed, as      chief now.  So for them, it's a move that I think has a lot of logic to      it.

Let's talk a little bit about the special role of the chief      justice. What, in fact is the--obviously all of the Supreme Court      justices are incredibly powerful in shaping legal policy, but what does      the chief justice do?

I think some people overstate and others understate the      role of the chief justice.  One of the most important roles, of course,      if he or she is in the majority and if an opinion--they choose who will      write the actual opinion.  That's a very important, substantive piece of      power.  Chief Justice Rehnquist had an important role in that he has      changed the court's role dramatically from what it was when he joined the      court.  The court was hearing probably 160 or more cases in the '70s and      that--he's cut that number down to about 80 cases a year.  So they really      are very selective on what they hear, which means a lot of cases that      many people may think have merit will never get any attention before the      Supreme Court.

But other thing that's important, and Chief Justice Rehnquist did this      with great class and with great effect:  He really spoke strongly about      the importance of the independence of the federal judiciary, seeking pay      raises for judges who ironically--some federal judges are making less      money than my law students who graduate after being at a law firm and go      into private practice, and that's a serious concern.  But it also helps      to set the tone for the court in terms of where it's going to go.  Given      John Roberts' record as a judge and as a lawyer, it clearly will make      this court swing even further to the right than it might have been with      Chief Justice Rehnquist.  And my only quibble with my dear friend Ted      Shaw is that I think Roberts will serve not 30 years but perhaps 40.      With the changes in health and age and all of that, he will be there for      a very, very long time, and he will have a major impact on the direction      of the court as we look forward.

Charles, let me just ask you--I don't want to go too deep into      talking about Judge Roberts before we get to Rehnquist, but you say that      he, as a chief justice, will swing the court further right.  What makes      you believe that?

His record, his disposition, his views, his      associations, his opinions, the memoranda that he's written, whether in      the solicitor general's office or working in the White House or any other      capacity.  He has been consistently, unequivocally conservative in every      time he's expressed his points of view.  And there isn't a whole lot of      equivocation there.  Now he has a right to be conservative, and President      Bush won the election; he has the right to appoint him.  But we shouldn't      be fooled in thinking that Roberts is going to be anything different than      a conservative, based on his views about federalism, his views about      affirmative action, his views about Roe vs. Wade.  And our hope is that      he will follow the law as it has been established and not see this as an      opportunity to swing more decisively to the right.  But we shouldn't be      fooled.  He's a conservative.  That's who President Bush wanted to      appoint and that's who he has appointed, and that's who will be, I think,      the chief justice come October 3rd, 2005.

I want to lead both of you gentlemen through the legacy of      Chief Justice Rehnquist.  Let me start with you, Ted.  When William      Rehnquist was nominated as an associate justice to the bench by Nixon in      1971, there were questions about his role as director for the Republican      Party's Operation Eagle Eye, what was called a ballot security program.      Tell us a little bit, if you can, about what that was.  And was it      appropriate for a judge to be involved in that?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, there were questions about William Rehnquist's role in      monitoring voters in Phoenix, where he was in private practice, and there      were charges that he intimidated voters along with others.  And all of      that is in the record now, and I'm not sure this is the time to go back      and rehash all that.  I'll just say that Chief Justice Rehnquist has been      remarkably consistent over the years, from the time he was a law clerk      through the time you're talking about when he was in private practice,      through his time on the bench.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: I perhaps have one difference with my good friend, Charles Ogletree,      which is I'm not sure that John Roberts will actually be any more      conservative than Chief Justice Rehnquist was.  He was very conservative,      although I think that during John Roberts' time on the court, if he's      confirmed, we may see the court move even further to the right as      President Bush gets another appointment in addition to his, and there's      always the possibility of more appointments.  But Chief Justice      Rehnquist's vote was one that we at the Legal Defense Fund would have      been happy to have, but in almost every circumstance in major civil      rights cases, we didn't get that vote.  Now there were a few cases in      which he came our way.  The Miranda decision was widely expected by some      conservatives to be overruled.  Chief Justice Rehnquist did not go along      with that.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: But for the most part, he was a very difficult vote for us to get, but he      certainly had a tremendous impact on the court, on the jurisprudence.  He      started as an outlier when he was appointed to the court.  By the end of      his life, he was right there in control of a very conservative court that      may get to be even more conservative.
Ted, let me follow up and ask you about the affirmative action      cases that the chief justice ruled on.  How did he vote in the various      affirmative action cases that came before him?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, he was a reliable vote against affirmative action.  Most      recently in the Michigan cases, he certainly expressed his opposition to      affirmative action, although in one of the opinions, his position wasn't      as clear as perhaps it had been in some of the earlier cases.  But he      generally was very suspicious of affirmative action, if not antagonistic      to it, and that was consistent through--even before Michigan, the      contracting cases that were before the Supreme Court, the Adarand case      involving federal contracting and the Croson case involving the municipal      contracting in the city of Richmond. Although Justice O'Connor was seen      as the swing vote, obviously this was a Rehnquist court, and he was a      formidable intellect.  So what he said had had effect.

Let me ask you, Charles, about minority clerks.  Judge      Rehnquist never hired a single African-American among the 82 clerks that      he had; 81 of those 82 were white, and he said, you know, `Wait for the      demographics to change.  There's no need for a wider net.  The system is      working just fine.' In your role as a Harvard law professor, do you find      that acceptable?  Do you find it acceptable that this pathway to the      inner workings of the justice system is--has essentially been for many of      the justices...

Well, let me say--answer this way:  Regrettably, Chief      Justice Rehnquist was not the only Supreme Court justice to not hire      African-American clerks.  And, in fact, some of our liberal friends who      served on the courts in earlier times also did not hire African-American      clerks.  The good news is, despite what Rehnquist has said and failed to      do, is that many members of the court, from Justice Stevens and Justice      Breyer, in particular Justice O'Connor, other judges have hired      African-American clerks, and it's a much better day.  I've had a number      of students who are exceptional.  They're not, you know, special admits      or special qualified folks.  They're really brilliant students, and I'm      glad that the court is having a little bit more diversity.

But that is a problem because you want the court to look like America.      You want the law school to look like America.  You want the law firms to      look like America, and that's one of the disappointments.

About Rehnquist, though, let me just say this about the legacy.  First of      all, when he was initially ill, I sent a leader to him expressing my deep      regrets about my illness, and I sent my condolences out to his family      now.  He was a very brilliant man.  He was number one in his his class at      Stanford.  He actually wrote a brilliant essay for a book that Deborah      Rhode at Stanford and I co-edited called "Brown @ 50," talking      about--praising Earl Warren, who wrote the unanimous decision in Brown      vs. Board of Education in 1950.  He handled the impeachment hearings of      President Clinton with excellence.  His public scholarship on the courts      and society were phenomenal.

But Ted is right; his decisions is where it made a difference.  He was      the Lone Ranger.  He was out there in dissent.  He wrote--he was in the      majority in Bush vs. Gore that stopped the vote in Florida in 2000,      against affirmative action in the Michigan case, one of the two      dissenters in Roe vs. Wade.  He has carefully and effectively over the      last 33 years cut back on exclusionary rule, given police more power and      suspects less power.  And when it comes to racial profiling, people have      to be very concerned that the court has moved in a very, very      conservative area that provides less protection for people than before.      So that's part of the legacy.  It's a mixed legacy, but when it comes to      issues of race and justice, I think folks are going to be less      congratulatory and more critical.  But the overall legacy will be shaped      up as someone who stuck by his views over a very, very long period of      time.

Let me ask you about whether or not the Bush administration is      going to feel pressure to nominate a woman or a person of color or both      for Sandra Day O'Connor's seat.  Sandra Day O'Connor herself expressed      some dismay that a woman was not nominated.  Now that Judge Roberts is      being nominated for the supreme Supreme seat, if you'd put it that way,      is the Bush administration going to feel pressure to take a second look      at the diversity of the court?

I think they'll feel pressure, but that means nothing.      Laura Bush appealed to him.  The Hispanic community appealed to President      Bush and he seemed to be taking those views into consideration, but he      nominated John Roberts, not Edith Clement, not Alberto Gonzales.  So I      think there will be pressure, but he doesn't have to run again, and he      wants to formalize his legacy as a president.  And I think even though      there will be pressure, that won't ultimately influence his choice.

I think what's interesting is that if the Roberts hearing, since it's      been elevated, is as contentious and as demanding as we anticipate, we      may see on Monday, October 3rd, Justice Sandra Day O'Connor as the ninth      justice, and she will serve until there's a replacement.  That's not a      bad thing for her to continue in that role, but I think that ultimately      the president will nominate a second person, and I hope that he does look      at the court and make sure that his legacy, as he claims it was in Texas,      as he promised it would be in the White House, as he's done with Colin      Powell and Condoleezza Rice and Alberto Gonzales and others--that the      court will look much more diverse with talented people who are diverse in      gender and ethnicity, and that should mean that someone, unlike the men      who are white on the court, will join the court and add some diversity      sometime after October.
Ted, what do you think the chances are for more diversity on      the court?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, I think that there will be some pressure in the minds of      some to appoint a Latino or a woman, a Latina, or something like that,      but I agree with Charles.  I don't think that the president is going to      feel a lot of that pressure.  He's going to appoint whom he wants to      appoint.  In my view, my concern isn't so much whether we have a Latino,      another African-American or a woman.  That's important.  I don't mean to      say that it's not, but I want somebody on the court who, although they're      conservative, is fair, open-minded, whose vote is in play, who will hear      the arguments, who does not come to the court with a mission-driven      agenda.  That's what the Legal Defense Fund said we wanted with respect      to the Roberts nomination. It's what we want with respect to any justice.      That's important.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: I do want to take this moment, though, to say that we also send out our      condolences on a personal level to the Rehnquist family.  Whatever      disappointments we had with getting the chief justice's vote, this is a      time for us to recognize that they've suffered a loss and the nation is      in mourning, and we join folks in sending condolences.

Let me--We're running out of time now--just ask a broader      question, which is, you two gentlemen, obviously, are legal experts,      legal scholars, and legal issues have always been inextricably tied to      the advancements of African-Americans in this country.  How important is      it for ordinary citizens to understand these decisions that the court      makes?  They're always very complicated and they flash across the front      pages.  What can people do to better educate themselves about these      decisions?

Farai, I think that's the most important question,      because we keep thinking that the Supreme Court is this high and supreme      entity that's removed from the people.  But I remember a slogan--I think      it's in the Florida Supreme Court--that said:  The court is where the      injured flock for justice. And I think the court is very important in      every aspect of our lives.  Our rights of privacy, whether we're going to      be taxed, whether we can get an education or a job, whether we face      discrimination.

And so even though those 80 decisions may not impact us every single day      in every single way, the court does enact the supreme law of the land,      and I think that we need to see it as more important.  We knew before      November 2004 that whoever became president would select two, three or      maybe even four Supreme Court justices by 2009, when the term officially      ends for the presidency.  So it's very important and it affects our      everyday lives.  Cases like what's going to happen to the tragedy that's      going on in the Gulf Coast and Florida and Alabama and Louisiana and      Mississippi now--that's going to come before the court in some way;      questions about whether or not the terrorism concern that's of      international concern will have some domestic impact on people's rights      of privacy.

All right.  I'm going to have to stop you there.      Unfortunately, Ted, I don't have another second.  I just want to thank      you both so much.  We are going to obviously keep on this story of the      Supreme Court as it evolves. Ted Shaw, president and director-counsel for      the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, and Charles Ogletree, law professor at      Harvard University.  Thank you, gentlemen, for joining us.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (President and Director-Counsel, NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Thank you.
Thank you.
You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.

Kimberly Samuels and her husband have been organizing bus trips to get displaced voters to the polls in New Orleans. A number of leading Civil Rights groups have teamed to make sure every eligible New Orleans voter who wants to vote can. Their campaign includes a voter's outreach hotline, public service announcements, and voter empowerment centers in cities like Atlanta and Houston.

We're joined know by Ted Shaw, director counsel and president of the NAACP legal defense fund. He joins us here in our New York Bureau, and at our headquarters in Washington, D.C., Barbara Arwine, executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law is with us. I thank you both. We greatly appreciate it. Barbara, let me start with you.

When you hear from a woman like Kimberly Samuels, and you hear all of what she has gone through, talk to us about the bigger picture of the importance of making sure that this election is fair and just.

speaker_label: Ms. BARBARA ARWINE (Executive Director, Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law)
text: What's beautiful about the Kimberly Samuels story is just how determined she is to vote, and how she's, you know, struggled with her life problems, and how she is still committed to her city. The problem that we have out there throughout the nation is that so many of the evacuees from New Orleans, some 90,000 to 120,000 registered voters spread out over 47 states, many who are still fighting for just basic life realities--where they're going to live, how they're going to pay the next rent, how they're going to buy groceries, where their children are going to be in school next semester--all of these really crushing life problems. And on top of it, they've got to think about voting.

speaker_label: Ms. BARBARA ARWINE (Executive Director, Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law)
text: So, one of the things that we've done, and why Ted and I are here today, is that we really believe so strongly that people need help, that they need assistance and that we don't want them worrying about all of those things Kimberly said about when they should vote, how they should vote. So, we set up, you know, two very beautiful resources that people can use. One is the hotline, the 1-866-OUR-VOTE hotline, which is 1-866-687-8683. And we tell people all of the time, you know, use the hotline. Call people, because there's lawyers who are trained, who are there for no other purpose but to help you vote on the other side, and can give you all the information you want. And Ted will describe the beautiful Web site, the Katrina Vote Web site that has also been set up.

Ted, talk to me about that, and also talk to me again about the bigger picture here. There are a lot of people who say this is all well and good, but what does this mean to me in Ohio? What does this mean to me in Florida? What does this mean to me in California? And to a great degree, this has bigger implications than just New Orleans.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-counsel, and President of NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, it does, Ed. And the Web site to which Barbara was referring is called Katrinavote.org. And all of the information about the election and the procedures, the deadlines, everything is in that Web site, and I encourage people to use that as well as the hotline, 1-866-OUR-VOTE hotline.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-counsel, and President of NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: The big picture is this, there are people spread out throughout a Diaspora of New Orleanians who are all over the country. And, in some places, they're concentrated in significant numbers, and some not as many numbers. But this is something that is unprecedented. We've never seen this kind of crisis, and there are people who are still New Orleanians who plan on returning to New Orleans. And they have a right to participate in choosing their representatives. They've lived there, many of them, most all of their lives. So they have as much at stake in New Orleans as anybody else who is there now. Now, the other thing is is that New Orleans is being remade, and people are aware of that. And some people think that a new New Orleans, in order to be better, has to be less black--has to be whiter, to be direct about it. We believe that everybody, regardless of race, regardless of wealth, has a right of return, and everyone has a right to participate in a democracy there.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-counsel, and President of NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: As many of us keep saying, if we were able to set up out-of-nation polling places for Iraqis in the United States to vote in the first democratic elections in Iraq, we could go a long way, including setting up out-of-state polling places, which the court has refused to order and the state has refused to do, to promote democracy here at home.

Barbara Arnwine, isn't it also important to make sure that these people, who have already felt disenfranchised, don't do so through this process? Many of them, right now, feel that this is and there are hindrances to their ability to cast their vote.

Yes, and I think it's critical that people, if they're in Houston, Atlanta, Massachusetts, Chicago, Seattle--that they're all aware that they can vote from where they're living right now, that they do not have to come to New Orleans, that they actually can call and receive an--request an absentee ballot by phone, that they can fax the request for that absentee ballot, that that absentee ballot can be faxed to them. They can fill it out, sign it, and fax it back. So it's very important for people to be aware that you don't have to lose your voting rights just because you can't come back to New Orleans on April the 22nd, which is this Saturday, when the election is being held.

But people who want an absentee ballot, they need to make that request as soon as possible. And that's why if they want to get help about how to make that request, how to proceed--they need to go to the hotline, the 1-866-OUR-VOTE hotline or 1-866-687-8683--and they can have people who can help them figure out how to get their absentee ballot. The one thing we don't want happening is in a big election year, like '06, we do not want it to start off with massive disenfranchisement of African-Americans. That would be an ominous sign, and we can't have that. And this, by the way, is the primary on Saturday.
Ted, with about 30 seconds to go, as Barbara suggests, we want to make sure that people understand that this is just the beginning.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-counsel, and President of NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Well, that's right, and the primary's on Saturday. On May 20th, the general election will be held, and people, who are properly registered to vote can vote in both of those, and should vote in both of those.

All right. Barbara Arnwine, executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law, and Ted Shaw, director-counsel and president of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, I thank you both for joining us.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-counsel, and President of NAACP Legal Defense Fund)
text: Appreciate it.
Thank you, so much, Ed.
Coming up next, indictments come down in the Duke Lacrosse case; and five black students are arrested in a fraternity hazing incident. We'll discuss these topics and more on our roundtable, up next.

For the other side of the story, I spoke with Ted Shaw, who was leaving the courthouse at the time. He is director-counsel and president of the NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund. He was also integrally involved in fighting these cases.
I asked him if he thought this ruling was the last nail in the coffin of programs that take race and America's legal racial - America's legacy of racial discrimination into account.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: No. That was a fear that many of us shared. And today's opinion, certainly, are deeply troubling and in some respects, they lost because the two school districts that were at issue, Seattle and Louisville had their plan struck down and there are five votes that seemed to see these kinds of plans as unconstitutional.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: On the other hand, rather than a 5-4 split, this is more of a 4-4-1 split. It's reminiscent of the Supreme Court's decision en banc with Justice Powell's opinion bridged two camps. Justice Kennedy clearly rejects the proposition that Chief Justice Roberts and three other justices would have held that race can never be considered in assignment of public school students and that the school districts could do nothing to try to desegregate or integrate or to maintain or achieve diversity.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: He doesn't buy that. He thinks that there's still a compelling state interest in having racial integration in public schools and doing something about de facto segregation, as it's called, that exist.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: But the window is still left open. But, you know, it's still a troubling set of opinions.
To follow that point, Chief Justice Roberts wrote in his majority opinion that, quote, "The way to stop discrimination is to stop discriminating." How practical is that?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: The problem with that supposition is that it holds that trying to desegregate or integrate public schools - trying to include people is racial discrimination that is tantamount to the discrimination that black folks and other people of color suffered under the regime of white supremacy and that's simply a false assumption.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: If Chief Justice Roberts and those who agree with him have their way, we would be preempted from doing anything about continued racial inequality unless we could prove that the specific actor engaged in intentional racial discrimination in a very clumsy way that's clearly not enough.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: Look, one of the most powerful moments that I've seen in the Supreme Court occurred today and that was the dissent read from the bench of Justice Breyer, a lengthy, powerful dissent that I think anyone who's concerned about racial justice and the Supreme Court should read.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: But he says, before he put this is the context of our continuing struggle to overcome both our history and continuing racial inequality for one reason or another, there are four justices of the court who simply don't see that.

Ted, your 25 years with the Legal Defense Fund career is coming to an end in February with your resignation. Rulings like this, do they discourage you, particularly, coming at the time that they do with regard to your own personal career?

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: Well, first of all, while I am going to leave the Legal Defense Fund in 2008, I will never step away from the issues that I have devoted my life to and that I care about. And I refused to be discouraged. In fact, what happens is that they get my blood flowing. It convinces me that we have to redouble our efforts. We have to continue to fight, and there are moments when I may be tempted sometimes to be discouraged but I know that when that happens, we might as well lay down that the other side wins. So I've learned that hope is not serendipitous. It's a choice. And we have to chose hope and then work to make that hope reality.
Ted Shaw, thank you so much for coming on. We appreciate it.

speaker_label: Mr. TED SHAW (Director-Counsel; President, NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund)
text: Thank you.

Ted Shaw is director-counsel and president of the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. We also talked with Democratic presidential candidate John Edwards yesterday before the Supreme Court announced its decision. The former senator from North Carolina admitted he was worried about several recent rulings by the high court.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN EDWARDS (Former Democratic Senator, North Carolina)
text: I am very concerned about it. If you look at what's happening with the court, there are many 5-4 decisions, which are moving in the direction of taking away the rights, taking away civil rights, taking away the rights of women, taking away the rights of minorities.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN EDWARDS (Former Democratic Senator, North Carolina)
text: And so I think that we have great reason to be concerned. It's a great indicator, by the way, of how crucial it is for my party to win the White House in 2008 because the next president's going to have huge control over the shape of the U.S. Supreme Court.
Again, that was Democratic presidential candidate John Edwards. To hear our complete interview, tune in tomorrow.

And one last note before we leave this segment, in California's 37th Congressional District, the death of Congresswoman Juanita Millender-McDonald in April left a power vacuum in the district that includes parts of Compton, South L.A. and Long Beach, but a special election earlier this week has cleared things up a bit.
African-American Assemblywoman Laura Richardson of Long Beach bested 17 other candidates. The Democrat is heavily favored to win a runoff election is scheduled for August 21st.
